meta.title: Aeva Technologies (NASDAQ: AEVA): How Co-Founder and CEO Soroush Salehian Is Commercializing FMCW 4D LiDAR as the Sensing Backbone of Autonomous Trucking, Passenger ADAS, and Industrial Precision — From Apple Special Projects Alumni Startup to Exclusive Daimler Truck Supplier and Top-10 European OEM Development Partner
meta.abstract:
Aeva Technologies, Inc. is a Mountain View, California-based developer of frequency-modulated continuous wave (FMCW) 4D LiDAR sensors and perception software. Founded in December 2016 by Apple Special Projects veterans Soroush Salehian and Mina Rezk, Aeva built its platform around a fundamental insight: that FMCW radar principles, applied through silicon photonics at 1,550-nanometer optical wavelengths, yield a LiDAR sensor measuring three-dimensional point position and instantaneous radial velocity at every pixel simultaneously — a capability conventional time-of-flight architectures cannot match in a single scan cycle. The company went public via SPAC merger in March 2021 at an approximately $2.1 billion post-deal valuation and transferred from NYSE to the Nasdaq Global Select Market in January 2025.

This dossier thesis rests on three interlocking strategic narratives. First, Aeva converted its core technology advantage into landmark commercial relationships: an exclusive long-range LiDAR supply agreement with Daimler Truck and Torc Robotics — valued at more than one billion dollars over its term — targeting start of production for the Freightliner Cascadia autonomous trucking platform in 2026 and commercial truck sales in 2027; and a development award from a global Top-10 European passenger-car OEM targeting 2028 start of production for a global vehicle platform outside China. Together, these agreements define Aeva's near-term revenue trajectory and validate the Atlas and Atlas Ultra product families. Second, Aeva has systematically extended its FMCW platform into industrial metrology and defense: shipping Eve 1D sensors to SICK AG and LMI Technologies, executing a multi-year production agreement with Nikon for the APDIS MV5X industrial metrology system, and expanding a contract with Forterra for autonomous defense ground vehicles. Third, NVIDIA's selection of Aeva Atlas as a reference 4D LiDAR sensor for the DRIVE Hyperion autonomous-vehicle compute platform — alongside $50 million strategic investments from both LG Innotek and an unnamed Fortune 500 technology subsidiary — signals ecosystem-level endorsement of FMCW as an emerging automotive sensing standard.

At the frozen snapshot date of May 23, 2026, Aeva had reported Q1 2026 revenue of $6.3 million, up ninety percent year-over-year, and guided for full-year 2026 revenue of $30 million to $36 million. Non-GAAP operating losses ran approximately $25–26 million per quarter against total liquidity of $224.5 million. The central analytical tension of this dossier is whether Aeva's technical differentiation and landmark design wins can translate into scaled, margin-positive revenue before the capital runway compresses, and whether FMCW will displace time-of-flight architectures across the automotive supply chain in the volumes required to sustain a near-$2 billion market capitalization.

chapters.title: The FMCW Bet: Aeva's Strategic Position at the Frozen Snapshot
chapters.body:
On the morning of May 23, 2026, Aeva Technologies carried a market capitalisation of approximately $1.77 billion on the Nasdaq Global Select Market — a figure that encoded a striking set of contradictions. The company had just reported first-quarter revenue of $6.3 million, up 90 percent year-over-year, and had guided the full year to $30–36 million. Against those numbers, the $1.77 billion valuation implied a forward revenue multiple of roughly 49 to 59 times — a pricing level that had no conventional justification in present-period financials and every justification in what the market believed was coming. Total liquidity stood at $224.5 million, composed of $99.5 million in cash and marketable securities and $125 million in an undrawn facility. At a non-GAAP operating burn of approximately $25–26 million per quarter, the runway was real but finite: eight to ten quarters at current rates, assuming revenue did not scale appreciably and no additional capital was raised. The tension between a near-billion-and-three-quarter valuation and a $6 million revenue quarter is not a paradox — it is the central fact of Aeva's existence at the snapshot date, and the question this dossier is structured to interrogate.

## Why FMCW Is Not an Incremental Improvement

To understand what Aeva is selling — and why its customers are paying a premium for exclusivity rather than shopping on price — requires a brief excursion into sensing physics. The dominant LiDAR architecture in the automotive industry is time-of-flight: a laser pulse is fired, reflects off a surface, and returns to a detector; distance is calculated from the round-trip travel time. ToF systems are mature, increasingly manufacturable, and capable of producing dense point clouds at acceptable range. What they cannot do is measure velocity directly. A ToF sensor must compare successive frames — subtracting one point cloud from another — to infer that an object is moving and estimate its speed. In high-density urban traffic or at highway closure rates, the latency and computational overhead of that frame-differencing approach introduce real-world limitations that are not engineering problems awaiting better processors; they are architectural constraints.

Aeva's frequency-modulated continuous wave architecture eliminates this constraint at the hardware level. Rather than emitting discrete pulses, an FMCW sensor transmits a laser signal whose frequency is continuously chirped — swept across a range. The returning signal is mixed coherently with the outgoing signal; the frequency difference between the two encodes both the distance to the target and, through the Doppler effect, the instantaneous radial velocity of that target. Every pixel in every scan delivers range, bearing, and velocity simultaneously, in a single pass, without any frame comparison. An autonomous vehicle equipped with FMCW LiDAR does not need to wait for a second frame to know that the vehicle ahead is decelerating at 0.3 g; it knows in the same scan that detected the vehicle's presence. The operational implication — faster threat classification, earlier intervention, reduced false-positive rates — is not marginal. It is the argument Aeva has made to every OEM customer since 2019, and it is the argument that produced two exclusive supply agreements by the snapshot date.

## Three Bets, One Architecture

The commercial strategy that Aeva had executed by May 2026 was built on three interlocking narratives. The first and largest is the exclusive multi-year supply agreement with Daimler Truck and its autonomous trucking subsidiary Torc Robotics, under which Aeva is the sole long-range LiDAR supplier for the Freightliner Cascadia autonomous platform. The contract has been characterised publicly as exceeding one billion dollars in total value. Start of production for autonomous-capable Cascadia trucks is targeted for 2026, with commercially sold autonomous trucks on U.S. roads targeted for 2027. Production-intent Atlas sensors were delivered to Torc in the first quarter of 2026, marking the transition from development to pre-production validation.

The second narrative is the development award from a publicly unnamed global Top-10 European passenger-car OEM, which designated Aeva as exclusive Tier-1 LiDAR supplier for a global vehicle platform outside China. Atlas Ultra — unveiled at CES 2025 — is the nominated sensor, targeting Level 3 ADAS in a behind-windshield integration. Start of production is scheduled for 2028. First Atlas Ultra prototype sensors were delivered to the European customer in the first quarter of 2026.

The third narrative operates on a shorter time horizon and a different commercial logic: industrial and defense revenue generated through the Eve 1D precision displacement sensor, the multi-year Nikon APDIS MV5X production agreement, and an expanded defense contract with Forterra, a Teledyne FLIR subsidiary supplying autonomous ground vehicles. These programmes do not move the revenue needle at the scale of a production automotive programme, but they generate recurring cash inflows, validate the FMCW platform in demanding non-automotive conditions, and reduce Aeva's dependence on automotive programme timelines that are, by their nature, difficult to compress.

## The Central Tension

The analytical question that unifies all three narratives is temporal. Aeva's non-GAAP burn of approximately $25–26 million per quarter runs against $224.5 million in total liquidity. Revenue must scale from the $30–36 million guided for 2026 toward a trajectory that approaches operating self-sufficiency — or the company will need to raise additional capital, potentially at dilutive terms, before its flagship automotive programmes reach full production volumes. The Daimler Truck SOP is targeted for 2026–2027; the European OEM SOP for 2028. Whether Aeva's capital runway can bridge the gap between today's pre-production deliveries and tomorrow's volume production invoices is the question on which the investment thesis turns.

The thirteen chapters that follow examine each dimension of that question in detail: the founding and technology genesis, the commercial proving ground from 2016 through 2026, the financial architecture of the business, the competitive landscape, the management team and governance, and the scenario analysis that frames Aeva's range of possible outcomes.

chapters.title: From Apple to Mountain View: The Founding, SPAC, and the Architecture of Ambition
chapters.body:
## The Convergence at Apple's Skunk Works

For four years, Soroush Salehian and Mina Rezk occupied adjacent corners of one of the most closely guarded engineering programs in Silicon Valley. Apple's Special Projects Group — the internal organisation believed to be developing autonomous vehicle technology under the internal codename Project Titan — assembled an unusual mix of disciplines: automotive engineers, computer vision researchers, and, critically, specialists in photonics and sensing. Salehian, who had joined Apple in February 2012 as a Manager of Product Development following two earlier startup exits, and Rezk, who arrived with deep expertise from Nikon's precision optics and sensing division, shared an intellectual preoccupation that the dominant LiDAR paradigm of the mid-2010s had not yet answered.

The problem was architectural. The time-of-flight sensors then commanding the autonomous vehicle sensing market — built largely around spinning laser arrays from Velodyne — measured range by timing a pulse of light from emission to return. They were effective but limited: they produced position and bearing, and nothing else per pixel. Velocity had to be inferred across successive frames, introducing latency. Worse, they were promiscuous to interference: a second LiDAR sensor, a bright sun, or a highly reflective surface could saturate the detector. Neither Salehian nor Rezk found this architecture satisfying as a foundation for mass-market automotive safety.

What they recognised, drawing on principles well-established in fiber-optic telecommunications and radar, was that coherent detection offered a different path. Frequency-modulated continuous wave (FMCW) sensing — in which a laser's frequency is swept in a controlled chirp rather than pulsed — had been exploited for decades in long-haul optical communications and military radar systems to extract not just range but instantaneous velocity from the Doppler shift embedded in a returning wave. The physics were mature. The manufacturing challenge was to miniaturise a technique that had historically required expensive bulk optics into something compatible with automotive production volumes and price points.

Silicon photonics was the enabling technology. By fabricating optical waveguides, splitters, and coherent detectors onto standard CMOS-compatible wafers through foundries like Tower Semiconductor, the core optical circuit — Aeva's proprietary CoreVision photonic integrated circuit — could be manufactured with the same yield economics as a semiconductor chip. Salehian and Rezk left Apple in late 2016 and incorporated Aeva Technologies in Delaware in December of that year.

## Seed Capital to Strategic Validation

The company's first external capital, a $3.5 million seed round in 2017, was modest by Silicon Valley standards but sufficient to prove the silicon photonics stack in a laboratory environment. The more consequential financing came the following year with a $45 million Series A led by Lux Capital and Canaan Partners — two investors whose portfolios encompassed deep-technology hardware bets with long development cycles. The round signalled that institutional capital was prepared to underwrite FMCW LiDAR as a credible alternative to time-of-flight architectures, not merely a research curiosity.

Strategic investments from Porsche SE and Lockheed Martin arrived in subsequent rounds, carrying a different kind of validation. Porsche SE's involvement connected Aeva to the Volkswagen Group ownership structure and its global passenger-vehicle programs. Lockheed Martin's stake pointed to a parallel market thesis: that FMCW's interference immunity and velocity-per-pixel capabilities had utility in defense and government applications well before autonomous consumer vehicles reached mass production. Together, these investments sketched out the multi-vertical commercial logic that Aeva would articulate more explicitly at the time of its public listing.

## The SPAC Window

By the autumn of 2020, the special purpose acquisition company had become the instrument of choice for autonomous vehicle technology companies seeking to access public capital without the quarterly scrutiny of a traditional IPO roadshow. Luminar Technologies, Ouster, Innoviz Technologies, and Velodyne Lidar all reached or approached public markets through SPAC mergers or direct listings within an eighteen-month window spanning 2020 and 2021. For early-stage hardware companies with limited revenue and multi-year commercialisation timelines, the structure offered a pragmatic shortcut: a defined capital raise, a faster path to a public currency for talent and acquisitions, and an investor base primed for growth narratives.

In November 2020 Aeva announced its agreement to merge with InterPrivate Acquisition Corp. (NYSE: IPV), a blank-check vehicle. The transaction was structured to deliver $243 million from the SPAC trust alongside $120 million from a concurrent private investment in public equity (PIPE) anchored by institutional investors. The merger closed on March 12, 2021, and Aeva's shares began trading on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker AEVA on March 15, 2021, at a post-deal equity valuation of approximately $2.1 billion. For a company that had not yet recognised meaningful product revenue, the market was pricing in the promise of FMCW LiDAR's commercial trajectory across automotive, industrial, and defense verticals simultaneously.

## The Reckoning

The euphoria proved short-lived. Beginning in late 2021 and accelerating through 2022 and into 2023, the cohort of LiDAR companies that had gone public during the SPAC wave underwent a severe re-rating. The immediate trigger was the sector-wide recognition that the timelines projected in SPAC investor presentations — in which fully autonomous vehicles would reach commercial deployment and generate material LiDAR volumes within two to three years — were not materialising. The broader Federal Reserve tightening cycle, which compressed multiples for pre-revenue technology companies across the market, compounded the effect.

Several of Aeva's peers encountered existential pressure. Ouster and Cepton were absorbed by competitors. Innoviz and others executed emergency financing rounds at steeply dilutive terms. For Aeva, the post-listing period required a recalibration between ambition and runway. The company undertook headcount rationalisation, narrowed its near-term product portfolio priorities, and concentrated engineering resources on the Atlas platform as the successor to the earlier Aeries development sensors. Contract manufacturing partnerships — principally Jabil for sensing system assembly and Fabrinet for optical subassembly — were selected to decouple production scale from fixed capital expenditure, preserving flexibility as automotive program timelines remained uncertain.

The share price, which had traded in double-digit territory in the weeks following the NYSE listing, fell sharply and sustained losses through 2022 and 2023, reflecting both the company-specific revenue trajectory and the broader destruction of value across the LiDAR sector.

## Capital Markets Housekeeping

Two administrative milestones bracketed the inflection that followed. On March 18, 2024, Aeva effected a one-for-five reverse stock split. The board's rationale was straightforward: a share price that had declined far from its post-SPAC highs risked triggering minimum bid-price deficiency notices from ~~exchange regulators~~ ==the NYSE and limited the company's compliance with the exchange's continued-listing price criteria== and limited the company's access to certain categories of institutional investment. The reverse split consolidated the share count without altering the underlying economic interests of existing shareholders, restoring the stock to a price range more consistent with the institutional equity universe.

Eleven months later, on January 16, 2025, the company announced its intention to transfer its listing from the NYSE to the Nasdaq Global Select Market. Trading on Nasdaq commenced on January 28, 2025, under the unchanged tickers AEVA for common stock and AEVAW for warrants. The board characterised the move as intended to increase visibility with the technology-sector institutional investors whose mandates are more naturally aligned with Nasdaq-listed companies in the semiconductor and automotive technology space.

## The Daimler Inflection

Neither milestone was as consequential as the commercial development that ~~closed out 2024~~ ==Aeva had already disclosed in February 2024 with its FY2023 results==. The announcement of an exclusive multi-year supply agreement with Daimler Truck and its autonomous trucking subsidiary Torc Robotics — designating Aeva as the ~~sole long-range LiDAR supplier for the Freightliner Cascadia autonomous platform~~ ==long-range and ultra-long-range LiDAR supplier for Daimler Truck's series-production autonomous commercial vehicle program== — transformed the company's narrative in a single disclosure. The contract, publicly characterised as exceeding one billion dollars in cumulative value over its duration, was the kind of concentrated, exclusive design win that Aeva's strategy had always targeted: a single high-volume platform, a locked-in position, and a start-of-production timeline — 2026 for autonomous-capable trucks, 2027 for commercially deployed autonomous vehicles on U.S. roads — close enough to be modelled with reasonable precision.

For a company that had spent three years navigating the post-SPAC discount, the Daimler Truck agreement served as something more than a revenue signal. It was an external validation, from one of the world's largest commercial vehicle manufacturers, that FMCW 4D LiDAR had cleared the supplier qualification bar for a safety-critical production program. The founding thesis — that coherent detection was the durable sensing architecture for autonomous transportation — had, in at least one measurable commercial instance, proved out.

chapters.title: The Atlas Family and the FMCW Platform: Products, Technology, and the Sensing Architecture
chapters.body:
## A Different Kind of Light

Every LiDAR system begins with the same physical premise: illuminate a scene with laser light, collect what bounces back, and infer the geometry of the world. Where Aeva Technologies diverges from the industry mainstream lies in how it processes that returning light — a distinction with consequences that extend from fundamental physics through to the architecture of autonomous vehicles.

The dominant commercial approach is pulsed time-of-flight. A laser fires discrete pulses; a detector measures how long each pulse takes to return. Range is computed directly from that interval. Velocity, however, is not measured — it is inferred, calculated as the derivative of successive range readings across consecutive scan frames. That inference introduces latency, and latency is hazardous when the object in question is a pedestrian stepping off a curb or a vehicle cutting across a highway lane at relative closing speeds that can exceed 150 miles per hour.

Aeva's FMCW — frequency-modulated continuous wave — architecture addresses this at the physics layer. Rather than pulsing, the system emits a continuous laser beam whose frequency is swept linearly upward and then downward in rapid chirps. When this frequency-chirped signal reflects off an object and returns to the sensor, it has acquired a phase shift relative to the transmitted beam. In a heterodyne detection scheme, the returning signal is mixed optically with a local copy of the transmitted beam; the resulting interference pattern produces a beat frequency proportional to the round-trip travel time, yielding range. Simultaneously, any radial motion between the sensor and the target imposes a Doppler frequency shift on the return. Because the up-chirp and down-chirp segments of the waveform respond to Doppler in opposite directions, solving the two equations jointly produces both range and instantaneous radial velocity from a single return signal — no cross-frame inference required, no latency-dependent extrapolation.

The practical consequence is that every pixel in an Aeva scan carries four data dimensions: X, Y, Z spatial coordinates and a direct velocity vector. This is the origin of the "4D LiDAR" designation. A vehicle equipped with an Aeva sensor can detect that a car is moving toward it at 30 miles per hour in the same instant it resolves the car's position, without waiting for the next frame. At the detection ranges that matter for highway driving — 200 to 500 meters — the reaction time delta between instantaneous and inferred velocity can represent the difference between a successful emergency braking event and a collision.

FMCW carries two further operational advantages. Because the detection scheme is coherent — it relies on the phase relationship between transmitted and received light rather than raw intensity — it is inherently immune to incoherent interference. Sunlight, regardless of intensity, does not share the phase structure of the transmitted chirp, and returns from competing sensors operating at the same wavelength lack the precise frequency relationship required to produce a valid beat signal. Retroreflective blooming, a well-documented failure mode in which high-reflectivity road signs saturate conventional ToF detectors and blind them to nearby lower-reflectivity targets, is similarly suppressed.

## From Discrete Optics to Silicon Photonics

The physics of FMCW coherent detection have been understood and exploited in fiber-optic communications and radar systems for decades. The challenge Aeva's founders identified — and the engineering achievement that constitutes the company's most durable moat — is integrating the optical components required to generate, transmit, and coherently detect a chirped laser signal into a form factor manufacturable at automotive cost structures.

A conventional FMCW system built from discrete optical components — laser source, beam splitter, local oscillator, photodetectors, fiber couplers — occupies the volume of a laboratory bench. Aeva's CoreVision photonic integrated circuit (PIC) miniaturizes the core optical functions of the coherent detection scheme onto a single chip, fabricated by Tower Semiconductor through the same silicon photonics foundry processes used to manufacture components for fiber-optic transceivers. The manufacturing pathway matters as much as the miniaturization: Tower Semiconductor's fabs operate at volumes that serve the telecommunications industry, meaning that the per-unit cost curve for CoreVision scales with semiconductor production economics rather than with the handcraft economics of precision optomechanical assembly.

The miniaturization trajectory across Aeva's sensor generations quantifies the commercial translation of that chip-scale integration. The Aeries I sensor, used in early customer development programs including Audi AID and the initial Volkswagen Group engagements, established the FMCW automotive proof of concept. Aeries II reduced the sensor footprint by 75 percent relative to Aeries I — a compression that enabled OEM integration discussions to become realistic rather than aspirational. Atlas, the current production-intent platform, reduced form factor a further 70 percent relative to Aeries II. The cumulative compression across two generations is sufficient to cross a threshold that matters enormously to passenger-vehicle OEMs: a sensor small enough to install behind a windshield, concealed from view, rather than mounted externally in the pod configurations typical of early autonomous-vehicle development programs.

## The Atlas Family

Atlas is the automotive mass-production sensor at the center of Aeva's commercial strategy. Production-intent Atlas units entered delivery to Torc Robotics — Daimler Truck's autonomous trucking subsidiary — in Q1 2026, constituting the first production-intent volume shipments under the exclusive supply agreement that designates Aeva as Daimler Truck's sole long-range LiDAR provider for the Freightliner Cascadia autonomous platform.

Atlas Ultra extends the performance envelope. Unveiled at CES 2025, Atlas Ultra targets 500-meter maximum detection range and 250-meter range for low-reflectivity targets — a specification that addresses one of the key operational requirements for Level 3 and Level 4 highway automation, where decision horizons extend well beyond the 200-meter range envelope of most competing long-range sensors. The sensor is engineered for behind-windshield integration, eliminating the external mounting hardware that adds aerodynamic drag, creates styling constraints, and presents a failure-mode surface for physical damage. First prototype Atlas Ultra samples were delivered to the unnamed Top-10 European OEM customer in Q1 2026, with volume production scheduled for H1 2026 and start-of-production for the OEM's global vehicle platform targeted for 2028. Atlas Orion constitutes an additional variant in the Atlas family, with specific performance positioning that complements the core Atlas and Atlas Ultra configurations within multi-sensor vehicle architectures.

Integrated with every Atlas-family sensor is the Aeva X1 onboard perception processor. Rather than offloading raw point-cloud data to a central vehicle compute stack, the X1 processes the sensor's outputs at the edge, delivering pre-processed object detections and velocity vectors that reduce the compute load on the vehicle's central processing unit. In the context of the NVIDIA DRIVE Hyperion reference design selection — Aeva's second selection to the DRIVE Hyperion platform, confirmed in Q1 2025 — the X1's outputs interface directly with NVIDIA's AV compute stack, a validated compatibility pathway that carries indirect weight with the OEM customers evaluating DRIVE Hyperion as their AV compute architecture.

## Omni and the Full-Vehicle Sensor Suite

The Atlas sensors address the long-range forward detection requirement. The Omni wide-angle sensor, unveiled at CES 2026 in partnership with LG Innotek, addresses a distinct and complementary requirement: 360-degree near-field coverage for low-speed ADAS and parking applications. Where Atlas Ultra looks 500 meters down a highway to detect a decelerating truck, Omni sweeps the full perimeter of a vehicle to detect a cyclist approaching from the side at an urban intersection or a pedestrian walking behind the vehicle in a parking garage.

The LG Innotek partnership is structurally significant beyond the product itself. LG Innotek brings automotive-grade volume production capacity for sensor hardware — the same manufacturing scale it deploys for camera modules and other automotive optical components — alongside up to $50 million in committed investment. The Omni product is a joint development; production volumes are planned for H2 2026. Within a complete vehicle sensor architecture, Omni and Atlas are additive: the Atlas family provides the long-range directional sensing required for highway automation decisions, while Omni provides the spatial awareness required for low-speed maneuvering, automated parking, and urban environment perception.

## Eve and the Industrial Proving Ground

The Eve platform launched commercially in Q1 2025 with the Eve 1 and Eve 1D precision laser displacement and speed sensors, targeting factory automation, robotic inspection, and precision metrology. The FMCW architecture that enables instantaneous velocity measurement in automotive contexts provides equivalent value in industrial settings: a displacement sensor that can simultaneously return micron-level positional accuracy and real-time velocity without requiring multi-frame differentiation is directly applicable to high-speed production line inspection, where parts move at speeds that defeat conventional measurement techniques.

SICK AG and LMI Technologies each placed initial orders exceeding 1,000 units upon the Eve 1D launch — a combined first-quarter volume that provided early commercial validation and a manufacturing ramp signal to Aeva's contract partners. The Nikon relationship, which predates the Eve 1D launch, represents a more mature industrial production benchmark: Nikon's APDIS MV5X industrial metrology system incorporates an earlier Aeva FMCW module under a multi-year production agreement that has been renewed through the current period.

## CityOS, Defense, and the Platform Coherence Argument

CityOS, Aeva's intelligent transportation software platform, and the company's defense sensor applications share a common architectural lineage with the automotive and industrial product families. CityOS deploys fixed-infrastructure FMCW sensors to deliver real-time traffic analytics, pedestrian safety monitoring, and vehicle speed measurement for municipal operators — a context in which the same interference immunity that protects automotive sensors from sunlight saturation provides consistent performance in outdoor infrastructure settings. A large-scale Georgia deployment executed in Q1 2026 extended the CityOS customer base beyond the earlier Sensys Gatso Australia and D2 Traffic Technologies relationships.

Defense applications — primarily autonomous ground vehicle obstacle detection for Forterra, with historical engagements at Lockheed Martin and NASA — leverage existing Atlas-family hardware rather than requiring dedicated defense-specific designs. The contract with Forterra was expanded in Q1 2026, providing incremental revenue and operational field data from demanding off-road environments that simultaneously enriches Aeva's detection algorithm development.

## Roadmap and Revenue Cadence Implications

The Atlas Ultra production ramp timeline disclosed in public filings carries specific implications for 2026 and 2027 revenue cadence. With first samples delivered to the Top-10 European OEM customer in Q1 2026 and volume production scheduled for H1 2026, the transition from development-services and prototype-unit revenue to production-volume product revenue for the passenger OEM relationship is positioned to begin registering in reported financials before the end of calendar 2026. The Daimler Truck / Torc Robotics program follows a parallel trajectory: production-intent Atlas deliveries in Q1 2026 precede the Freightliner Cascadia start-of-production target of 2026, with commercially sold autonomous trucks on U.S. roads targeted for 2027.

The behind-windshield integration capability of Atlas Ultra is more than a packaging convenience. For the passenger OEM design win — a global vehicle platform launch in 2028 — behind-windshield installation is a prerequisite for the kind of seamless consumer-grade integration that differentiates a production vehicle from a development mule. The physics enabling that form factor — the chip-scale integration of FMCW coherent detection through Tower Semiconductor's silicon photonics foundry — is the same architecture that originated in a Mountain View garage in 2016. What has changed is the scale: from laboratory prototype to exclusive Tier-1 supplier contract, the FMCW platform is entering the phase where its commercial value is measured not in engineering milestones but in unit deliveries.

chapters.title: Doubling Revenue, Deepening Losses: The Financial Architecture of an Early-Commercial LiDAR Company
chapters.body:
## The Revenue Doubling Machine

Few financial profiles in the technology sector are as arithmetically clarifying as Aeva Technologies'. The company generated $4.3 million in revenue in fiscal year 2023. That figure doubled to $9.1 million in 2024, doubled again to $18.1 million in 2025, and arrived at $6.3 million in the first quarter of 2026 alone — a 90 percent year-over-year increase. Management guided full-year 2026 to $30–36 million, implying a third consecutive year of near-doubling. Against a backdrop of exclusive design wins at Daimler Truck and a Top-10 European passenger OEM, the growth rate reads as validation of a thesis. Against the company's cost structure, it reads as the distance still to travel.

| Period | Revenue | YoY Growth |
|---|---|---|
| FY2023 | $4.3M | — |
| FY2024 | $9.1M | +112% |
| FY2025 | $18.1M | +99% |
| Q1 2026 | $6.3M | +90% |
| FY2026 Guidance | $30–36M | ~66–99% |

The arithmetic of the guidance range deserves examination. With Q1 2026 at $6.3 million, reaching the floor of $30 million requires the remaining three quarters to collectively produce $23.7 million — an average of $7.9 million per quarter, implying sequential step-ups of roughly 25–40 percent from the Q1 base. Reaching the midpoint of $33 million requires $26.7 million across Q2–Q4, or a back half of the year running at approximately $9–10 million per quarter. At the guidance ceiling of $36 million, Q4 alone would need to approach $11 million. That is achievable — but only if the Daimler Truck program sensor shipments, the Atlas Ultra deliveries to the European OEM, and the Eve 1D industrial ramp all accelerate in concert. The guidance is not implausible, but it is heavily back-loaded. At the Q1 annualised run rate of $25.2 million, the company would miss its own floor by approximately $5 million without material sequential acceleration.

## The Weight of the Cost Structure

The more sobering number sits on the other side of the ledger. Aeva spent approximately $61–65 million per year on research and development in the periods approaching fiscal 2025, and approximately $30–35 million on sales, general and administrative costs — an aggregate operating cost base of roughly $91–100 million annually before any consideration of cost of goods. Against a 2025 revenue base of $18.1 million, the proportional gap is severe: for every dollar of revenue recognised in FY2025, the company spent approximately $5 on operating expenses.

The Q1 2026 non-GAAP operating loss of $25.8 million, annualised, implies a run-rate operating cost structure of just over $100 million. If one assumes that the existing cost base remains approximately flat as revenue scales — a reasonable short-term assumption given that R&D headcount and infrastructure are already invested in the Atlas production ramp — then the implied non-GAAP break-even revenue threshold can be estimated as follows: with gross margins gradually improving but still modest, the company would need annual revenues somewhere between $90 million and $120 million to approach non-GAAP operating neutrality. At the current doubling cadence — $18.1 million in 2025, $33 million implied for 2026, $60–70 million extrapolated for 2027 — that threshold becomes theoretically reachable in 2028 only if the Daimler Truck and European OEM programmes begin generating volume-level product revenue. The mathematics are plausible but narrow, and depend on execution across multiple independent production ramps.

Full-year 2024 GAAP operating losses were $158.4 million; the non-GAAP figure was $123.2 million, reflecting the magnitude of the investment phase. The trajectory from those levels toward the Q1 2026 non-GAAP loss of $25.8 million — roughly $103 million annualised — represents modest operating leverage, but not a structural inflection.

## The GAAP–Non-GAAP Divide

The gap between Aeva's reported GAAP losses and its non-GAAP presentation is not trivial. In Q1 2026, the GAAP operating loss was $35.1 million against a non-GAAP loss of $25.8 million, implying approximately $9.3 million per quarter — or roughly $37 million annualised — in items excluded from the non-GAAP measure, principally stock-based compensation.

On a diluted share count of approximately 63 million shares, that annualised SBC burden equates to approximately $0.59 per share — a meaningful dilutive friction even by the standards of growth-stage technology companies. Expressed as a percentage of the $1.77 billion market capitalisation at the May 23, 2026 snapshot date, the annualised SBC represents roughly 2.1 percent of equity value per year in compensation-driven dilution. That figure will attract scrutiny from institutional investors as the company approaches the capital efficiency benchmarks that OEM programme economics require.

The non-GAAP presentation is standard practice in the sector and is offered alongside, not instead of, GAAP disclosures. Investors evaluating Aeva's trajectory should nonetheless read the GAAP figures as the economically complete picture: the $35.1 million quarterly operating loss reflects the actual cost of operating the business, including the equity compensation that represents a significant component of how the company attracts and retains the engineers building its FMCW platform.

## Capital Structure and Liquidity Management

Aeva entered the fiscal year 2025 with total liquidity of $237 million. By the end of Q1 2025, that figure had eroded to $206 million — a trough that, at the prevailing burn rate, represented a finite and visible clock. The recovery to $224.5 million by March 31, 2026, was not organic: it was driven by the two strategic investments completed in 2025.

In May 2025, an unnamed Fortune 500 technology subsidiary made a $50 million strategic investment, acquiring approximately 6 percent of Aeva's equity — a transaction that simultaneously brought capital and a commercial partnership in manufacturing and product commercialisation. In July 2025, LG Innotek formalised its strategic relationship with a commitment of up to $50 million, structured as a combination of equity stake and nondilutive capital, alongside a production capacity commitment and joint development of the Omni wide-angle sensor. Together, these two transactions contributed approximately $100 million in committed capital to the liquidity position, buying material runway at a moment when the company's organic cash generation remained deeply negative.

As of March 31, 2026, the $224.5 million total liquidity comprised $99.5 million in cash and marketable securities and a $125 million undrawn revolving or equity facility — a structural cushion that provides flexibility but whose drawdown mechanics and terms represent relevant investor disclosure. Net cash used in operations in FY2024 was $106.9 million; the FY2025 figure, not yet disaggregated in the available disclosures, is implied by the liquidity trajectory to have been partially offset by investment inflows.

## Gross Margin: Toward the Inflection Point

Aeva's gross margin history reflects the cost profile of a company transitioning from engineering-development revenue to early-volume product sales. GAAP gross margins were negative or near-zero in prior periods, reflecting manufacturing ramp costs, tooling absorption, and the accounting treatment of non-recurring engineering contracts. The mix between NRE and product revenue — not disclosed in granular detail at the snapshot date — matters significantly here: NRE revenue, which recognises milestone payments from development programmes, carries high incremental margins but does not recur; product revenue carries initially lower margins that improve as volumes scale.

The available disclosures indicate that non-GAAP gross margins have been improving and that product gross margins on Atlas and Eve 1D sensors were approaching positive territory as of the Q1 2026 reporting period. Whether they crossed into positive territory on a sustained basis remains to be confirmed in subsequent filings. The entry into positive gross margins would represent a qualitative inflection — not because the contribution is material at current volumes, but because it signals that the manufacturing cost curve has been crossed and that incremental revenue begins to reduce, rather than compound, the operating loss.

## Valuing a Promise: Revenue Multiples and Sum-of-Parts

At $1.77 billion in market capitalisation against trailing twelve-month revenue of approximately $20.97 million, Aeva traded at roughly 84 times trailing revenue as of the May 23, 2026 snapshot. On the FY2026 guidance midpoint of $33 million, the forward revenue multiple compresses to approximately 54 times. These are not aberrant figures in the context of deep-technology hardware platforms at pre-scale commercialisation stages, but they are demanding, and they embed specific assumptions about programme timing that are not yet contractually certain.

| Valuation Frame | Market Cap | Revenue Basis | Multiple |
|---|---|---|---|
| Trailing TTM | $1.77B | $20.97M | ~84x |
| FY2026 midpoint | $1.77B | $33.0M | ~54x |
| FY2026 ceiling | $1.77B | $36.0M | ~49x |

A sum-of-parts framing, while speculative, is analytically instructive. The Daimler Truck exclusivity contract — publicly characterised as exceeding $1 billion in value over its duration, with SOP targeted for 2026–2027 — implies a revenue stream that, at any reasonable discount rate and risk-adjusted probability, would justify a substantial portion of the current market capitalisation on its own. The European OEM development award, targeting SOP in 2028 on a global vehicle platform, adds a second revenue vector that could, at volume, dwarf the trucking contract in aggregate units. The industrial business — Eve 1D, Nikon APDIS, and the CityOS infrastructure deployments — is generating revenue now and is structurally decoupled from automotive programme timelines, providing a base that reduces the binary character of the automotive thesis. The present market capitalisation implies that investors are pricing some probability-weighted combination of all three vectors materialising on schedule.

## The Runway Question

At the Q1 2026 non-GAAP operating loss of $25.8 million — the cleanest proxy for quarterly cash consumption — the $224.5 million in total liquidity represents approximately 8.7 quarters of runway before the company would need either additional capital or a material reduction in the cost base. Against the $99.5 million in immediately accessible cash and securities, that figure compresses to approximately 3.9 quarters, underscoring why the $125 million undrawn facility is not merely a conservative balance sheet item but a functional operational necessity.

The scenario under which Aeva avoids dilutive capital raising before its flagship programmes reach production volumes requires several conditions to hold simultaneously: FY2026 revenue lands at or above the guidance midpoint; FY2027 revenue accelerates toward $60–70 million as Daimler Truck volume deliveries begin; gross margins turn durably positive, reducing the incremental cash consumed per unit of revenue; and operating expense growth remains moderate, allowing revenue to close the gap on the cost base. In this scenario, the company approaches a self-sustaining operating profile — still loss-making on a GAAP basis, but with cash generation from operations sufficient to fund the residual R&D investment required to sustain the Atlas and Eve platforms — sometime in the 2027–2028 window.

Should the Daimler Truck SOP slip, or should the European OEM award encounter development delays, the revenue acceleration required to stay within the current liquidity envelope becomes materially harder to achieve. In that scenario, a capital raise — structured either as an equity offering, an expansion of the existing facility, or a new strategic partnership — would likely be necessary before the end of 2027. The company's demonstrated ability to attract strategic capital from LG Innotek and the Fortune 500 technology subsidiary on commercially rational terms suggests that such a raise, if required, would not be a distressed transaction. But it would dilute existing shareholders at multiples that depend entirely on the programme milestones standing between now and that decision point.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
## A Revenue Multiple Built on Option Value

At $28.13 per share on approximately 63 million diluted shares as of May 23, 2026, Aeva Technologies commanded a market capitalisation of approximately $1.77 billion. Against trailing-twelve-month revenue of $20.97 million, that figure implies an EV/Sales multiple — netting the company's $99.5 million in cash and marketable securities against its enterprise value — of roughly 79 times. Against the midpoint of the company's own FY2026 guidance of $30 to $36 million, the forward EV/Sales compresses to approximately 49 to 58 times. These are not multiples derived from conventional cash-flow analysis. They are, in effect, option prices: the market is not paying for what Aeva earns today but for what its exclusive OEM contracts could produce once they enter serial production.

No GAAP earnings exist, and none are expected before the decade is out under even the most optimistic modelling. EBITDA is deeply negative — non-GAAP operating losses ran approximately $25.8 million in the first quarter of 2026 alone, implying an annualised cash consumption of roughly $100 million against a revenue base approaching $25 million annualised. A price-to-earnings ratio or EV/EBITDA multiple is arithmetically undefined; the valuation toolkit applicable here is limited to price-to-sales and scenario-based DCF framing anchored to the programme revenues expected when Daimler Truck and the Top-10 European OEM reach start of production.

## Where the Stock Sits in Its Own History

Aeva went public via SPAC in March 2021 at an implied post-deal equity value of approximately $2.1 billion — essentially where the stock trades five years later, though the path between those two points was anything but straight. The 2021–2022 sector-wide de-rating of EV, AV, and LiDAR names compressed Aeva's market capitalisation to a fraction of its listing value; multi-year lows were reached in 2023 and early 2024, when the broader LiDAR cohort was being re-priced from "autonomous future" optionality to "prove the revenue" scepticism. The 1-for-5 reverse stock split of March 2024 — designed to maintain institutional investor eligibility and Nasdaq compliance — crystallised how far the share price had fallen from its listing-era highs.

The recovery from those lows to a 52-week range of $8.83 to $38.80 as of the snapshot date was driven by a discrete sequence of catalysts: the Daimler Truck exclusivity agreement (publicly characterised as exceeding one billion dollars in total potential value), the Top-10 European passenger OEM development award in Q4 2024, the NVIDIA DRIVE Hyperion reference design selection in Q1 2025, and the LG Innotek and Fortune 500 strategic investments that together committed up to $100 million in capital by mid-2025. Each catalyst re-rated the stock not because near-term revenue changed materially but because the probability-weighted present value of the production-era contract was revised upward.

The current $1.77 billion capitalisation is therefore best understood as a re-convergence with the 2021 SPAC listing value, reached by a different route: where 2021 was pure narrative, 2026 carries actual exclusive supply agreements, delivered prototype sensors, a growing industrial revenue line, and strategic backing from LG Innotek and an unnamed Fortune 500 manufacturing partner.

## Peer-Group Multiples: The Comparison That Makes AEVA Look Expensive — and Why Investors Accept It

The relevant public-market peer group is narrow. The post-2022 LiDAR shakeout eliminated several once-prominent names; Velodyne and Ouster merged, Cepton was acquired, and several SPAC-era entrants were wound down or taken private. The survivors, and their approximate valuation parameters as of the snapshot date, are shown below. Peer figures are estimated from publicly available filings and market data; exact figures may differ from reported results.

| Company | Ticker | TTM Revenue (est.) | Market Cap (est.) | EV/Sales (TTM, est.) | Key Differentiator |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Aeva Technologies | AEVA | ~$21M | ~$1.77B | ~79x | FMCW 4D; Daimler Truck exclusive |
| Luminar Technologies | LAZR | ~$80M | ~$300–400M | ~4–5x | ToF long-range; Volvo/Mercedes programmes |
| Innoviz Technologies | INVZ | ~$15M | ~$80–120M | ~6–8x | ToF solid-state; BMW Series 7 |
| Hesai Group | HSAI | ~$220M | ~$700–900M | ~3–4x | High-volume ToF; China automotive |
| Mobileye Global | MBLY | ~$2.0B | ~$12–14B | ~6–7x | Camera/radar ADAS; Intel heritage |

The disparity between Aeva's EV/Sales and every named peer is substantial. Luminar, which carries significantly more revenue and its own OEM relationships including Volvo and select Mercedes platforms, trades at roughly one-fifteenth of Aeva's revenue multiple. Hesai, the dominant supplier to Chinese automakers with volumes that dwarf the Western cohort, commands barely four times revenue. The gap is not a pricing anomaly: it reflects the market's specific assessment of the Daimler Truck exclusivity premium. If autonomous Class 8 trucking on U.S. highways reaches commercial scale on the 2026–2027 timeline embedded in the contract, Aeva's per-mile sensing economics — as sole long-range LiDAR supplier on the Freightliner Cascadia — generate a revenue profile that is structurally unlike any other pure-play LiDAR name. The market is assigning Aeva a premium for contract structure, not for current revenue density.

## What the Price Implies: A DCF Reading

Working backward from the $1.67 billion enterprise value, a conventional DCF framing requires the market to expect substantial revenue scale and margin improvement over the next five to eight years. At a 15 percent discount rate — appropriate for a pre-profit hardware company with binary programme risk — and assuming a terminal EBITDA margin of 20 percent (consistent with mature automotive component suppliers), the current valuation implies revenue of roughly $500 to $700 million by 2030 and approaching $1 billion by 2032. Neither figure is implausible: the Daimler Truck contract alone, if autonomous trucking penetrates even modestly into the Class 8 fleet at $2,000 to $5,000 per sensor per truck, could approach $200 to $400 million in annual revenue by the early 2030s. The European OEM programme compounds this if its 2028 SOP holds.

The critical input is not the terminal multiple but the probability that production programmes arrive on time and at anticipated volumes. The market appears to be assigning roughly 40 to 60 percent probability that both major automotive programmes execute broadly on schedule — a meaningful discount to an unconstrained base case, but equally a meaningful premium above what current revenues would justify.

## Bull, Base, and Bear Scenarios

**Bull case — $55 to $80 per share.** Daimler Truck begins autonomous Cascadia production in 2027 on schedule. The European OEM programme confirms its 2028 SOP. Industrial Eve 1D revenue grows to $40 to $60 million by FY2027 as SICK AG and LMI Technologies expand orders and new customers are added. Total revenue reaches $150 to $200 million by FY2027 and $400 to $500 million by FY2029. The market re-rates Aeva to 10 to 15 times 2028 forward revenue as line-of-sight to positive EBITDA becomes credible. Implied market capitalisation: $3.5 to $5.0 billion, or $55 to $80 per share on the diluted share count.

**Base case — $22 to $35 per share.** Revenue meets the FY2026 guidance midpoint of $33 million and grows to $70 to $90 million in FY2027 as Daimler production ramps slowly and industrial contributes $20 to $30 million. The European OEM programme confirms 2028 SOP but volumes remain unquantified. Non-GAAP operating losses narrow but remain above $15 million per quarter through FY2027, requiring the company to draw on its $125 million undrawn facility. The stock holds at 40 to 50 times FY2027 forward revenue — roughly flat to the snapshot valuation — as investors maintain option value without triggering a re-rating. Implied range: $22 to $35.

**Bear case — $5 to $10 per share.** Autonomous trucking faces regulatory or operational setbacks that push meaningful Daimler Truck volume beyond FY2028. The European OEM award is delayed or scoped down. Revenue reaches $40 to $50 million by FY2027 but operating losses are not reduced, forcing a dilutive equity raise. The LiDAR sector de-rates as investor patience with pre-profit hardware names shortens. At 5 to 8 times revenue on a $50 million base, enterprise value falls to $250 to $400 million, implying a share price of $4 to $7 on a modestly diluted share count.

## The Gap Between Consensus and This Dossier

The market's current read, embedded in the $1.77 billion capitalisation, leans toward the base-to-bull corridor: it is not pricing perfection, but it is pricing material programme execution. The principal risk the stock price underweights is time. Each quarter of delay in Daimler Truck autonomous production burns $22 to $26 million in non-GAAP cash and compresses the runway without expanding the revenue base. If the 2026 SOP slips to 2028, the present value of the production contract declines materially, and the liquidity buffer — $224.5 million as of March 31, 2026 — may require supplementation at inopportune terms.

The dossier's read is that the bull case is real but narrower in probability than the stock's premium implies. The Daimler relationship is genuine, the FMCW technical differentiation is durable, and the industrial pivot provides a meaningful revenue floor. But autonomous trucking at commercial scale on U.S. public roads remains a regulatory and operational achievement, not merely an engineering one. A base valuation of $25 to $32 per share appears supportable on programme-risk-adjusted assumptions; the upper range requires both flagship programmes to execute without material delay across a three-year window — a bar that no LiDAR company has yet cleared at mass-production scale.

chapters.title: The Quarterly Cadence: Management Commentary, Revenue Beats, and the Commercialization Narrative
chapters.body:
The quarterly earnings calendar became Aeva Technologies' most consequential communications platform as the company transitioned from development-stage credibility to commercial-stage delivery. Each successive quarter from late 2024 through early 2026 added a layer of evidence to management's central claim: that FMCW 4D LiDAR had cleared the threshold from prototype to production, and that the revenue trajectory accompanying that transition was real, repeatable, and building.

## Q4 2024: The Daimler Quarter and the Guidance Reset

The fiscal fourth quarter of 2024 closed with what management would describe as a structural inflection point. The Daimler Truck exclusive supply agreement — designating Aeva as the sole long-range LiDAR supplier for the autonomous Freightliner Cascadia platform under the Torc Robotics programme — had been publicly confirmed, providing the first billion-dollar-contract anchor to an investor narrative that had previously rested almost entirely on technology differentiation.

Full-year 2024 revenue came in at $9.1 million, up 112% from $4.3 million in FY2023, establishing a pattern of near-doubling that management would carry forward as a guiding narrative. GAAP operating losses for FY2024 were $(158.4) million; non-GAAP operating losses $(123.2) million — figures that underscored how far the commercial revenue base still sat from the company's cost structure. Total liquidity at year-end 2024 stood at $237.0 million.

On the Q4 2024 earnings call, chief executive Soroush Salehian framed the coming year in terms that would later be tested against actual results:

> "2025 is the year where Aeva will be in a strong position...deliver a year of record revenues with significant growth."

The statement was deliberately un-specific on quantum, but the directional commitment was firm. Against the actual FY2025 delivery of $18.1 million — 99% growth, the second consecutive year of near-doubling — that commitment was met with mathematical precision.

## Q1 2025: A Liquidity Trough, the Eve 1D Launch, and the NVIDIA Stamp

The opening quarter of 2025 arrived with two significant commercial catalysts but also the most acute liquidity anxiety the company had publicly navigated. Revenue for Q1 2025 came in at approximately $3.3 million — implied by the subsequent year-over-year disclosure that Q1 2026's $6.3 million represented 90% growth. Total liquidity declined to $206.0 million, down $31 million from year-end 2024, as quarterly non-GAAP operating losses ran in the $25–26 million range against a revenue base that had yet to scale.

Sell-side analysts pressed management on the burn-rate trajectory relative to the programme revenue ramp. The response was an explicit bridge narrative: two strategic investment processes were in progress, Salehian indicated, without disclosing counterparty names. The company described both as manufacturing and commercialisation partnerships intended to fund the runway to autonomous trucking start-of-production.

The positive datapoints flanking the liquidity question were substantial. In Q1 2025, NVIDIA selected the Atlas sensor as a reference 4D LiDAR for the [DRIVE Hyperion](https://investors.aeva.com/news-releases) autonomous-vehicle platform — the second NVIDIA reference selection for Aeva following an initial designation in 2022. The designation provided access to NVIDIA's OEM customer pipeline and third-party validation of the Atlas sensor's integration characteristics within a leading AV compute stack.

Simultaneously, Aeva commercially launched the Eve 1D industrial laser displacement sensor and announced purchase orders for over 1,000 units from SICK AG and LMI Technologies within weeks of product introduction. The industrial vertical, long positioned as a near-term revenue bridge decoupled from automotive programme timelines, had produced its first credible volume signal.

## Q2–Q3 2025: The Capital Bridge Closes

The two strategic investment processes that management had signalled in Q1 materialised in rapid succession. In May 2025, an unnamed Fortune 500 technology subsidiary completed a $50 million investment, acquiring approximately a 6% equity stake. In July 2025, LG Innotek formalised a partnership encompassing up to $50 million in capital — structured as a blend of equity and nondilutive contribution — alongside a commitment of LG Innotek manufacturing capacity and a joint development mandate for the Omni wide-angle sensor eventually unveiled at CES 2026.

The combined $100 million in committed capital reset the liquidity narrative. On successive quarterly calls, Salehian characterised both transactions as more than financial: the Fortune 500 partnership as a distribution accelerant into consumer electronics and industrial channels; the LG Innotek deal as a supply-chain de-risking move that reduced manufacturing concentration risk as Atlas production volumes were set to scale.

Quarterly revenue through the middle of 2025 continued to build, with approximate combined Q2–Q3 2025 revenue of roughly $9.2 million — implied by the full-year total of $18.1 million less the bookend quarters — representing a meaningful sequential progression of approximately $4.5–4.7 million per quarter.

## Q4 2025: Record Revenue and the Year Delivered

The fiscal fourth quarter of 2025 produced the strongest revenue quarter in Aeva's history: $5.6 million, carrying the full-year total to $18.1 million. Against Salehian's January 2025 commitment to "a year of record revenues with significant growth," the delivery was unambiguous. Full-year growth of 99% matched the pace of FY2024's 112% expansion, establishing two consecutive years of near-doubling.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue | YoY Growth |
|---|---|---|
| FY2023 | $4.3M | — |
| FY2024 | $9.1M | +112% |
| FY2025 | $18.1M | +99% |
| Q1 2026 (actual) | $6.3M | +90% YoY |
| FY2026 (guidance) | $30–36M | +66–99% implied |

The NVIDIA partnership — deepened through announcements at CES 2026 in January — was framed as extending beyond the Q1 2025 reference design selection into an active commercialisation arrangement, with management citing the integration as a pathway for Atlas to enter OEM validation programmes running on the DRIVE Hyperion platform.

## Q1 2026: Production Intent and the 2026 Guidance Frame

The first quarter of 2026 delivered $6.3 million in revenue — 90% above the prior-year period — and two programme milestones that management elevated in its earnings narrative. Production-intent Atlas sensors were delivered to Torc Robotics at Daimler Truck during the quarter, marking the transition from development sample to the pre-production specification units that feed automotive validation programmes ahead of 2027 commercial deployment. Simultaneously, the company completed first deliveries of Atlas Ultra prototype sensors to the unnamed Top-10 European passenger OEM, the counterpart to the trucking programme with a 2028 start-of-production target.

Management set [FY2026 guidance](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001789029/000095017025071752/aeva-20250331.htm) at $30–36 million. At the Q1 2026 quarterly run rate of $6.3 million, the guidance implied meaningful back-half loading — a pattern consistent with production ramps in which customer pull-through accelerates as validation milestones are cleared. Total liquidity at March 31, 2026 stood at $224.5 million, comprising $99.5 million in cash and marketable securities and $125.0 million in an undrawn facility. At the Q1 2026 non-GAAP operating loss of $25.8 million per quarter, the company carried eight to ten quarters of runway without additional capital raises.

## Analyst Coverage, the Price-Target Overshoot, and Narrative Quality

As of the May 2026 snapshot, five sell-side analysts covered AEVA with a consensus "Strong Buy" rating and a twelve-month price target of $24.10. Against the actual share price of $28.13, the stock had already outrun the aggregate analyst consensus by approximately 17%. The gap was not a function of scepticism — all five maintained the most bullish available designation — but of institutional and retail momentum pricing in the Daimler production ramp and European OEM programme timelines ahead of model updates. The 52-week range of $8.83–$38.80 illustrated how sharply the market's assessment of that probability had shifted since the Daimler announcement.

The price-target undershoot reflected a structural limitation in the available disclosure. Aeva had not provided a granular breakdown of revenue by customer, by product line, or by the proportion of product sales versus non-recurring engineering. Investors seeking to build bottoms-up financial models — projecting per-sensor volumes, per-unit average selling prices, and gross margins at programme scale — found the earnings narrative rich in milestone language but sparse on the unit economics that would anchor such projections. Management consistently framed Daimler as a billion-dollar-plus contract and the European OEM as a global vehicle platform, but neither per-unit ASP, per-programme quarterly shipment schedule, nor product gross margin by platform appeared in SEC filings or call transcripts through the Q1 2026 reporting period.

The result was an earnings narrative that communicated momentum credibly — consecutive revenue doublings, strategic partnership capital, production-intent deliveries against stated timelines — but left institutional investors unable to independently stress-test the path from $18.1 million in FY2025 revenue to a base capable of covering $100 million in annual non-GAAP operating costs. In the near term, that gap between qualitative conviction and quantitative modellability was absorbed by the market's willingness to price Aeva at roughly 97x trailing revenue. Whether that premium would be sustained through the automotive validation cycle, or recalibrated as programme timelines approached commercial inflection, remained the central tension in the commercialisation narrative entering the second half of 2026.

chapters.title: The Founders and Their Board: Co-Founder Control, Apple Alumni DNA, and the Governance of a Deep-Tech Bet
chapters.body:
## The Founders: Apple Alumni and the FMCW Hypothesis

The two men who founded Aeva Technologies in Mountain View in December 2016 arrived at the same insight from complementary angles. Soroush Salehian, who had studied mechanical engineering at Stanford University before co-founding two technology startups and joining Apple as a Manager of Product Development in February 2012, understood the systems integration and miniaturization demands of consumer hardware at scale. Mina Rezk, who came to Apple from Nikon's precision optics and sensing division, brought the deeper photonics expertise — the understanding of coherent light behavior that underpinned frequency-modulated continuous wave detection. Together, inside Apple's Special Projects Group, they identified a convergence opportunity: FMCW detection principles that had long powered fiber-optic telecommunications and military radar could, if implemented on photonic integrated circuits, produce an automotive LiDAR sensor with capabilities that time-of-flight architectures could not replicate. Both left Apple in late 2016 and incorporated Aeva Technologies.

The Apple parentage shaped the company's engineering philosophy — an emphasis on dense integration, miniaturization, and the elimination of discrete optical components in favor of monolithic photonic circuits — and it informed early hiring. [Salehian's Forbes 30 Under 30 recognition in 2018](https://investors.aeva.com) arrived during the seed-stage years, when the company had raised $3.5 million and was preparing a $45 million Series A led by Lux Capital and Canaan Partners. Rezk operated as the technical anchor — the person whose mastery of coherent optics determined whether the FMCW-on-chip hypothesis was achievable in silicon.

## Governance Concentration: Rezk's Threefold Role

The corporate structure the founders chose for a public company is unusual. As of the frozen snapshot date, Rezk simultaneously held the titles of Co-Founder, President, Chief Technology Officer, and Chairman of the Board — a concentration of operational and governance authority rare among post-SPAC public technology companies.

[Nasdaq Global Select Market listing standards](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001789029/000114036125016680/ny20046673x1_def14a.htm) require that a majority of the board consist of independent directors and that audit, compensation, and nominating committees be composed entirely of independent members. Aeva satisfies the letter of these requirements: five independent directors — Hrach Simonian, Stephen Zadesky, Dr. Stefan Sommer, Katherine Motlagh, and Daniel Gibson — constitute a majority of the seven-member board. What the structure does not provide is a conventional separation between oversight and execution. Rezk, as Chairman, presides over the body that in principle evaluates the management team of which, as President and CTO, he is a leading member.

No shareholder proposals seeking to separate the Chairman and CEO roles appear in the proxy materials reviewed for this chapter. The governance concentration has not generated visible investor activism — a circumstance that reflects both the limited float available to activist positions and the logic that, at the pre-production ramp stage, concentrating technical authority in the person most capable of executing is arguably value-enhancing rather than value-destructive.

## CFO Saurabh Sinha: Crisis Finance and Hardware Scale-Up

Saurabh Sinha joined Aeva as Chief Financial Officer in 2020, before the SPAC transaction closed, and has served through the full arc of the company's public-market existence. His résumé traces an unusually turbulent path. At InvenSense — the MEMS motion-sensing company acquired by TDK in 2017 — Sinha served as Corporate Controller, gaining direct exposure to scaling semiconductor-based sensing hardware through consumer-electronics supply chains. The parallels to Aeva's situation are direct: InvenSense operated at the intersection of precision manufacturing, consumer-device integration, and iPhone supply-chain competitive pressures.

The JUUL Labs chapter of Sinha's career demands careful reading. He served as Chief Accounting Officer and interim CFO at JUUL during 2018–2020, a period encompassing the company's peak $38 billion valuation, the FDA regulatory assault, and the wave of litigation over youth vaping that ultimately destroyed the vast majority of that value. Navigating that environment required financial discipline, investor communication under extreme adverse conditions, and capital allocation judgment in a cash-burning company facing existential regulatory risk. For a company managing a $224.5 million liquidity position against approximately $25–26 million in non-GAAP quarterly operating losses, Sinha's experience in managed financial crisis is directly relevant — provided the lesson he internalized at JUUL was disciplined capital management rather than growth-at-all-costs. Sinha holds an MBA from the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania.

## The Independent Directors: Expertise as Strategic Asset

The board's independent wing was substantially reconstituted in the twelve months ending May 2025, and the composition reflects a deliberate strategic architecture.

[Hrach Simonian](https://investors.aeva.com/corporate-governance/board-of-directors) has been a director since November 2017, representing Canaan Partners and serving as Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee Chair. His long tenure makes him the board's institutional memory, having observed the arc from garage prototype through SPAC to Nasdaq listing.

[Stephen Zadesky](https://investors.aeva.com/corporate-governance/board-of-directors), appointed November 2022 and Compensation Committee Chair, brought something specific that other directors could not: operational experience scaling Apple's most commercially consequential hardware program. As former Vice President of iPhone Engineering — one of the most demanding manufacturing integration roles in consumer electronics — Zadesky understands the gap between prototype performance and production-line reliability. His presence provides a sanity check on the engineering assumptions underpinning Aeva's 2026–2028 production ramp commitments.

[Dr. Stefan Sommer's](https://investors.aeva.com/corporate-governance/board-of-directors) November 2023 appointment was the most strategically charged. Sommer served as Chief Executive Officer of ZF Friedrichshafen AG — one of the world's largest Tier-1 automotive suppliers and an Aeva partner — until 2022. His network spans the European OEM procurement and engineering community at exactly the level at which Aeva's development awards are negotiated. The timing is notable: Sommer joined the board in November 2023, and the Top-10 European OEM development award designating Aeva as exclusive Atlas Ultra supplier was disclosed in the fourth quarter of 2024. Proxy materials contain no related-party disclosures linking his prior ZF relationships to the OEM award, and correlation does not establish causation. What his presence unambiguously provides is credibility in the Tier-1 conversation: a former ZF CEO on the board signals to European OEM procurement teams that Aeva has passed a threshold of industry legitimacy.

[Katherine Motlagh](https://investors.aeva.com/news-releases/news-release-details/aeva-adds-finance-and-infrastructure-leader-its-board-directors), appointed March 27, 2025 following Erin Polek's resignation, brings infrastructure-sector CFO experience from CyrusOne, American Tower, Ericsson, and Nokia — deepening the Audit Committee's financial governance depth at a moment when capital runway management is among the board's most consequential responsibilities.

[Daniel Gibson](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20250505284502/en/Aeva-Appoints-Leading-Technology-and-Public-Markets-Investor-to-its-Board-of-Directors), Founder and CIO of Sylebra Capital, joined May 1, 2025. His appointment, arriving in the same period as the unnamed Fortune 500 subsidiary's $50 million strategic investment, signals an institutional investor community actively engaging the governance layer. Whether Gibson's presence represents constructivist pressure to accelerate commercialization timelines or serves primarily as an information channel to a significant shareholder base remained, at the frozen snapshot, an open question.

## Compensation Structure and Equity Alignment

The gap between Aeva's GAAP and non-GAAP operating losses — approximately $35 million and $26 million per quarter respectively — is substantially explained by stock-based compensation running at roughly $9 million per quarter. The [DEF 14A proxy for fiscal year 2024](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0001789029/000114036125016680/ny20046673x1_def14a.htm) discloses that Salehian and Sinha receive compensation packages weighted heavily toward equity, with base salaries modest relative to peer-group benchmarks.

| Metric | Approximate Level (Q1 2026) |
|---|---|
| GAAP operating loss | ~$35M per quarter |
| Non-GAAP operating loss | ~$26M per quarter |
| Implied SBC | ~$9M per quarter |
| Total liquidity (March 31, 2026) | $224.5M |
| Annualized cash consumption (non-GAAP) | ~$100M |

This structure aligns executive incentives with long-term shareholder value in principle. The critical variable is whether vesting schedules are tied to commercialization milestones or are purely time-based — the former creates genuine alignment with the 2027–2028 automotive production start objectives; the latter does not.

## Key-Person Risk and Succession

The 10-K risk factor disclosures identify key-person dependency as a material risk, and the concern is grounded in operational reality. Salehian is the company's external face — managing investor relations, OEM commercial negotiations, and the public narrative around FMCW technology — while simultaneously serving as the internal strategic decision-maker. Rezk's specific expertise in coherent photonics, developed at Nikon and Apple and applied to the CoreVision chip architecture, sits at the center of the company's technical differentiation. Neither role has an obvious internal successor, and the proxy does not enumerate specific retention arrangements beyond standard equity vesting.

## Synthesis

The leadership configuration Aeva carried into its 2026–2028 production ramp combines genuine technical credibility with a governance architecture that demands clear-eyed assessment. The founding team's Apple Special Projects pedigree is the most plausible explanation for why FMCW-on-chip exists as a manufacturable product at all — the integration discipline required to move from coherent detection theory to a windshield-mountable production sensor is precisely what that environment trained. The CFO's InvenSense and JUUL background provides stress-tested financial instinct for hardware-at-scale economics. The board's independent wing, anchored by a former ZF Friedrichshafen CEO and a public-markets technology investor at the governance table, is better matched to automotive supplier execution than the typical post-SPAC residual board.

The governance concentration is a structural choice, not an oversight. At the current stage, when the technical execution of Atlas Ultra and the commercial execution of the Daimler Truck and Top-10 OEM agreements are the primary value drivers, concentrating authority in the people with the deepest relevant expertise carries an internal logic. The risk is temporal: as production volumes scale and organizational complexity grows, the architecture that today looks like disciplined focus may, in retrospect, reveal itself as fragility.

chapters.title: Exclusive Trucking, European ADAS, Industrial Metrology, and Defense: Aeva's Multi-Vertical Commercial Footprint
chapters.body:
## The Daimler Truck Anchor: Exclusive Long-Range LiDAR for Autonomous Class 8

The centerpiece of Aeva's commercial architecture is a supply relationship that, if it executes on schedule, would place the company at the heart of North American autonomous trucking. Disclosed in 2024, Aeva's exclusive multi-year agreement with Daimler Truck and its autonomous-vehicle subsidiary Torc Robotics designates Aeva as ~~the sole long-range LiDAR supplier~~==the exclusive long- and ultra-long-range LiDAR supplier== for the Freightliner Cascadia autonomous platform — a contract publicly characterized as exceeding $1 billion in aggregate value over its term. The commercial milestones are precise: autonomous-capable Cascadia trucks are targeted to enter production in 2026, with commercially sold autonomous vehicles operating on U.S. roads targeted for 2027. ~~Production-intent Atlas sensors were delivered to Torc in the first quarter of 2026, a milestone Aeva's management described as validating the transition from development hardware to volume-ready product.~~==Aeva delivered production-intent C-sample Atlas sensors to Daimler Truck and Torc in early 2026 for validation toward future series production.==

The revenue mechanics of a sole-source automotive supply agreement of this scale are structurally compelling. Class 8 trucks command substantially higher per-unit price tolerance than passenger vehicles, and long-range LiDAR is non-optional for highway autonomy at the detection distances required for safe braking at commercial vehicle speeds. While Aeva has not disclosed per-sensor pricing for the Cascadia program, industry benchmarks for automotive-grade LiDAR at SOP suggest unit economics in the hundreds to low-thousands of dollars per sensor at series-production volumes — implying meaningful per-truck content value that compounds rapidly across a fleet deployment ramp.
